nature-val-094.title: Revealed preference: judging people by their choices
nature-val-094.text: Economists have long faced a measurement problem. Utility, the satisfaction behind people's choices, cannot be measured directly. In 1938 Paul Samuelson proposed a way around it: watch what people choose and work backward. This is revealed preference. It assumes that people's preferences show in their purchasing habits. The logic is simple. If someone chooses bundle a when bundle b was also affordable, a is said to be revealed preferred to b. A bundle is just a set of goods, and affordable means within the person's {{ref:nature-econ-102}}. Rather than measure utility, economists defined it from observed behavior. The approach contrasts with {{ref:nature-val-102}}, which ask people directly, and economists usually trust revealed preferences more. It matters for nature because ecosystem services rarely carry prices. Methods such as {{ref:nature-val-092}} and {{ref:nature-val-088}} link a service to a market good to estimate {{ref:nature-econ-344}}. Critics raise two objections. A purchase cannot show which alternatives were given up, and the theory wrongly assumes preferences stay constant over time. Several economists, including Amartya Sen and Stanley Wong, go further. They call the theory tautological, true by definition, or a failed research program.

nature-val-087.title: Ecosystem valuation: putting numbers on nature's services
nature-val-087.text: In 1997 {{ref:nature-hist-048}} and colleagues made the first estimate of what the world's ecosystem services are worth: $33 trillion a year. Ecosystem valuation is the process behind numbers like that. It assigns a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides. The aim is practical. Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's flood control and carbon storage helps policy-makers compare policies through {{ref:nature-val-001}}. The tools come in two families. Survey methods, such as {{ref:nature-val-085}}, ask people what they would pay. Revealed preference methods, such as {{ref:nature-val-092}} and {{ref:nature-val-088}}, infer it from behavior. The results vary enormously. TEEB found values from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs. Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded. Many are also non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use leaves no less for others, and no one can be kept out. Some programs go on to pay landowners; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests. Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and that the money value of services depends on how income is distributed. Behind this lies a philosophical and ethical dispute over whether nature should be priced at all.

nature-val-092.title: Hedonic regression: reading value from house prices
nature-val-092.text: How much is a park worth to the people who live beside it? Part of the answer hides in their house prices. Hedonic regression treats a house as a bundle of features, such as bedrooms, lot size and distance from the city center, each with its own price. It breaks the sale price into contributions from each feature, usually with {{ref:nature-econ-257}}. In environmental work it measures how much a nearby amenity such as a park raises home prices, holding the other features fixed. Hedonic modeling was first published in the 1920s to value farm land, with roots also traced to Court's 1939 study of car prices. Today it is also used in real estate, marketing research and Consumer Price Index calculations. That last use is debated. Some critics argue it can understate US inflation, while studies abroad show that ignoring quality change can misstate inflation too.

nature-val-089.title: Willingness to accept: the price of putting up with harm
nature-val-089.text: Willingness to accept is the least money a person would take to sell a good, or to put up with a harm such as pollution. It is the counterpart of {{ref:nature-econ-344}}, the most a buyer would give up to get something or avoid something unwanted. Both are reservation prices, the limits past which a person walks away. A trade's price falls between the buyer's willingness to pay and the seller's willingness to accept, and the gap between them is the {{ref:nature-econ-338}}. Formally, it is the payment that leaves a person's utility after an unwanted change equal to their utility before it. Which measure applies depends on property rights. If lakeside residents have a right to a clean lake, what counts is the compensation they would accept for its pollution. It can be estimated with choice experiments or asked directly in {{ref:nature-val-085}} surveys.

nature-val-088.title: Travel cost analysis: valuing a park by the trip
nature-val-088.text: A park may charge no market price, but reaching it costs visitors time and money. {{ref:nature-hist-062}} suggested using that fact in a 1947 letter to the US park service. Travel cost analysis values a place without a market price, such as a park or beach, from what visitors spend to get there. People living farther away spend more to visit and come less often; those nearby visit more and spend less. Analysts group visitors into distance zones and use regression to relate each zone's visit rate to its travel cost. The result builds a {{ref:nature-econ-371}} for the site. The area under that curve gives visitors' willingness to pay, which serves as the site's value in {{ref:nature-val-001}}. Trice and Wood refined the method in 1958, and Clawson in 1959.

nature-val-095.title: The weak axiom: a rule for consistent choice
nature-val-095.text: Revealed preference needs a rule for what counts as consistent choice. The weak axiom of revealed preference supplies the basic one. If a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable. Stronger rules build on it. The strong axiom, SARP, adds that choices cannot be indirectly revealed preferred to each other. That preserves transitivity. Anyone who prefers a to b and b to c then prefers c least. The generalized axiom, GARP, extends SARP to cases where several bundles give equal utility, and rules out preference cycles.

nature-val-096.title: Afriat's theorem: from choices to a utility function
nature-val-096.text: In 1967 Sydney Afriat proved a useful result for anyone studying choices. A finite set of observed choices that satisfies GARP, the generalized consistency rule, can be explained by a utility function, a rule that scores each option. His inequalities go further and let that function be built directly from the data. SARP, by contrast, only proves such a function exists for infinite datasets. The theorem is widely used in econometrics to test rationality and to build preferences from real data.

nature-val-103.title: Benefit transfer: borrowing values from earlier studies
nature-val-103.text: When time and money rule out original research, benefit transfer offers a cheap way to value a project. It borrows the data, models and results of earlier studies of similar projects or sites. It comes in two forms. Value transfer moves a single unit value from an earlier site. Function transfer uses valuation functions drawn from many studies, and can be more accurate; {{ref:nature-nbs-095}} can help build one. Two errors lurk. Measurement error comes from biased study selection and assumptions. Transfer error arises when the original and new sites do not correspond.

nature-val-093.title: Replacement cost: what it takes to start over
nature-val-093.text: An insurer valuing a television can pay the price of a similar new one today. That is replacement cost: the amount needed, at today's prices, to replace something with an undamaged equivalent. It can differ from market value, and from 'actual cash value', which subtracts {{ref:nature-econ-519}}. The idea matters beyond insurance. In urban planning, the replacement cost of public infrastructure such as roads can push local governments toward bankruptcy.

nature-val-102.title: Stated preference: asking people what they value
nature-val-102.text: Sometimes the only way to learn what people value is to ask. Stated preference methods measure value through surveys rather than by watching what people buy. Ecosystem valuation divides its methods into this family and the revealed preference family. The best known is {{ref:nature-val-085}}, which asks people their willingness to pay for an ecosystem or one of its services. Survey-based choice experiments are also used, and David Hensher and Jordan Louviere are credited with the first stated preference choice models. Non-use values are usually measured this way, because people's market behavior reveals nothing about them. Many economists remain unconvinced. They question whether survey answers can be trusted, and prefer the evidence of binding market purchases. One middle path combines revealed and stated data to get the advantages of both.

nature-val-085.title: Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey
nature-val-085.text: In 1963 Robert K. Davis used a survey to value a wilderness area for hunters and tourists. It was the first application of contingent valuation, an idea S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup had proposed in theory in 1947. Contingent valuation puts a money value on things not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution. A survey usually asks how much people would pay to keep an environmental feature such as biodiversity. Or it asks how much they would need to be paid to accept its loss. That makes it a stated preference method, unlike methods that rely on prices people actually pay. It rose to prominence in the United States in the 1980s. Governments then gained authority to sue for damage to environmental resources held in trust for the public, including non-use values. The {{ref:nature-val-076}} was the first case where its surveys put numbers on damages. US government departments have since used it widely, for example to value river recreation below Glen Canyon dam. Critics warn of strategic answers, protest answers, response bias and respondents ignoring their income limits. Clive Spash found that many answers behaved like charitable donations rather than trade prices. Many economists therefore doubt that the answers reflect real values. Defenders reply that newer survey designs have fixed the early biases.

nature-val-086.title: The NOAA panel: can surveys be trusted?
nature-val-086.text: Could surveys of willingness to pay be trusted? The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration convened a panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, to judge. It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993. Its verdict was a cautious yes. Well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values. Good design meant personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats. Preferring cautious estimates, the panel advised asking willingness to pay to protect a good, not willingness to accept its loss.

nature-val-101.title: The embedding effect: when part and whole do not add up
nature-val-101.text: Willingness to pay for a project is larger when people are asked about it first than when it comes second. That is one face of the embedding effect. In contingent valuation, people struggle to value one public good that is part of a larger set of similar goods. Part-whole bias is related: what people would pay for two policies valued separately does not add up to what they would pay for both together. The effect suggests contingent valuation is not an unbiased measure of policy effects. One fix asks about the whole set first, then the named item's share.

nature-val-090.title: The WTA–WTP gap: selling dear, buying cheap
nature-val-090.text: Ziv Carmon and Dan Ariely found that willingness to accept for basketball tickets was more than 10 times willingness to pay. Standard theory predicts the two amounts should match. Yet people ask far more to give something up than they would pay to get it. One explanation is income limits on what people can pay. Another is the {{ref:nature-econ-033}}, where owning something triggers loss aversion. Plott and Zeiler argued the gap partly reflects participants misunderstanding the experimental task. Researchers still disagree. The answer matters for contingent valuation, where endowment effects are widespread.

nature-val-097.title: Compensating differentials: the extra pay for a bad job
nature-val-097.text: Risky jobs have to pay extra to attract workers. A compensating differential is that extra pay, offered so someone takes an unpleasant or risky job instead of other work. For an especially pleasant job it runs the other way: workers accept lower pay. The idea, credited to Adam Smith, has been used to study injury risk, the money value workers put on their own lives, and regional wage gaps. A hedonic wage function plots how wages rise with a job's undesirable features, such as the chance of injury. Economists expect lower wages in pleasant places, so wage gaps can reveal what an area's attractiveness is worth.

nature-val-091.title: Choice modeling: learning value from trade-offs
nature-val-091.text: Before the Bay Area Rapid Transit was built, Daniel McFadden used past transport choices to predict how many would ride it. The work earned him the 2000 Nobel economics prize. Choice modeling is the family of methods behind such forecasts. It models how a person or group decides, using real choices or choices stated in a set context. Usually it infers where items sit on a hidden scale, typically utility, from repeated choices of one option over another. Its roots lie in Thurstone's 1920s research on food preferences and in random utility theory, which McFadden developed in economics. A survey describes a good by attributes and levels. Combinations explode: a phone with 2 brands, 3 shapes, 3 sizes and 4 memory options has 72, so only a subset is shown. Respondents must weigh trade-offs, which lets analysts estimate an implicit price for each attribute. It is regarded as the best method for valuing quality improvements that vary in several dimensions at once.

nature-val-100.title: Discrete choice: modeling either-or decisions
nature-val-100.text: Which mode of transport to take is a choice between separate options, not a question of how much to buy. Discrete choice models describe and predict such decisions. A model gives the probability that a person picks each alternative, based on features of the alternatives and of the person. The models can be derived from utility theory, and only differences in utility between alternatives affect the probabilities. The first applications were in transportation planning; in market research the approach is commonly called {{ref:nature-val-098}}. Common forms include binary logit and {{ref:nature-val-081}}, multinomial, conditional and nested logit, and {{ref:nature-val-079}}. They are usually estimated by {{ref:nature-econ-239}}. Standard logit assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives, a substitution pattern that is not always realistic. The last model on the list relaxes it by letting tastes vary between people.

nature-val-098.title: Conjoint analysis: pricing a product's parts
nature-val-098.text: Products are bundles of attributes, and conjoint analysis asks which ones people really value. It is a survey-based statistical technique, mainly from market research. Respondents see a controlled set of products broken down by attribute. Their choices reveal the implicit value, or part-worth, of each attribute. Marketing professor Paul E. Green developed it, and Jordan Louviere pioneered the choice-based version that underlies discrete choice analysis. Because attribute combinations grow exponentially, fractional factorial designs cut the profiles respondents must judge. It is also called discrete choice modeling or stated preference research.

nature-val-082.title: Random utility: why rational choices look random
nature-val-082.text: Two people facing exactly the same options often choose differently. Classic economics assumes a rational person picks the alternative with the highest utility, which can be inferred from choices. A random utility model explains the variety. Each person's choices depend on a random, unobserved state. The model gives each person a distribution over utility functions rather than a single one, and assumes rational behavior given the hidden state. To an observer, the choices then look random. Choice experiments rest on this logic: how often item A is chosen over item B measures how much it is preferred. A popular version was developed by Luce and Plackett.

nature-val-080.title: Multinomial logit: choosing among many options
nature-val-080.text: Multinomial logistic regression predicts the probabilities of more than two unordered outcomes from a set of explanatory variables. It extends {{ref:nature-eco-582}}, and goes by many names, including multinomial logit, and softmax regression. In discrete choice theory, each outcome's score is read as the utility a person gets from choosing it. A random part stands for unmodeled factors. Used for choices, it assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives: the odds between two options do not depend on what other options are present. Many psychology studies show that people often violate this assumption. Even so, it is often the first stage of analysis in {{ref:nature-val-099}} studies, giving average utilities for items.

nature-val-076.title: The Exxon Valdez spill: putting a price on damage
nature-val-076.text: On March 24, 1989, the supertanker Exxon Valdez struck Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska. Over the next few days it spilled more than 10 million US gallons of crude oil. It was the first case where contingent valuation surveys were used in a quantitative assessment of damages, and use of the technique spread from there. Existence values were part of the legal damage assessment. An Anchorage jury awarded $287 million in actual damages and $5 billion in punitive damages, which an appeals court ordered reduced.

nature-val-081.title: The probit model: predicting yes or no
nature-val-081.text: Some outcomes take only two values, such as yes or no. A probit model is a regression model for such an outcome, built on the normal distribution, the bell curve. It estimates the probability that an observation with given characteristics falls into one of the two categories, the same problem {{ref:nature-eco-582}} handles. It can be motivated as a latent variable model: the outcome shows whether an unobserved variable is positive. It is usually estimated by maximum likelihood. Chester Bliss coined the term in 1934, though the basic model goes back to Fechner in 1860.

nature-val-079.title: Mixed logit: letting tastes vary
nature-val-079.text: Mixed logit lets tastes vary randomly between people, which makes it a fully general model for analyzing discrete choices. It overcomes three limits of standard logit. It allows random taste variation, unrestricted substitution patterns, and correlation in unobserved factors over time. It also drops the restrictive assumption of independence of irrelevant alternatives. With suitable specification it can approximate any random utility model of discrete choice to any accuracy. The price is computation. Its choice probability has no closed form, so it is estimated by simulation, drawing repeatedly from the taste distribution.

nature-val-099.title: Best–worst scaling: picking extremes
nature-val-099.text: Ask people to rate a list and every item risks being rated 'quite important'. Best–worst scaling avoids that. Respondents pick the best and the worst item from a subset of a longer list. The task repeats with subsets varied by a statistical design. Because people choose rather than rate, it avoids scale-use bias. Jordan Louviere invented it in 1987 at the University of Alberta, as a form of discrete choice experiment. Choices are usually analyzed with a random utility model. One difficulty remains: it is hard to combine best and worst answers when people use different decision rules for each.

nature-val-083.title: Scope neglect: when bigger harms do not count more
nature-val-083.text: In one study people would pay $80 to save 2,000 migrating birds from drowning in oil ponds. For 20,000 birds they offered $78, and for 200,000, $88. The harm grew enormously; the price barely moved. This is scope neglect, a cognitive bias in which the value people place on a problem does not grow in proportion to its size. Other willingness-to-pay studies have found a logarithmic relationship, where value rises ever more slowly, or no relationship at all. Daniel Kahneman explains it as judgment by prototype. People price a mental image, such as one oil-soaked bird, rather than the number affected. It is a specific form of extension neglect, closely linked to the 'mass numbing' studied by Paul Slovic. For contingent valuation, the lesson is uncomfortable.

nature-val-075.title: Cheap talk: words that cost nothing
nature-val-075.text: In {{ref:nature-econ-034}}, cheap talk is costless communication between players whose messages do not directly change the payoffs. It is non-binding and cannot be verified by a third party. A speaker could lie freely, but may choose not to. That sets it apart from signaling, where sending some messages can be costly. Whether talk helps depends on the game. In a coordination game, a round of cheap talk can help players reach better outcomes. In the Prisoner's Dilemma it is ignored.

nature-val-084.title: Hypothetical bias: saying is not paying
nature-val-084.text: Saying you would pay is not the same as paying. Hypothetical bias is the distortion in values people state in surveys about goods they do not actually have to pay for or give up. A public health study found it is greater when people have less information about a good and information is costly. When hypothetical bias is high, stated willingness to pay is lower, widening the WTA–WTP gap. John A. List studied whether explicit warnings remove it.

nature-val-077.title: Latent class models: finding hidden groups
nature-val-077.text: Answers to a political questionnaire could reveal hidden groups that match political camps. A latent class model is a statistical tool for finding such groups. It sorts multivariate discrete data, many category answers per person, into hidden classes. It assumes the data come from a mixture of distributions, with the variables independent within each class. It is called latent because each data point's class is not observed.

nature-val-078.title: Meta-regression: why studies disagree
nature-val-078.text: When many studies disagree, meta-regression tries to sort out why. It is a kind of {{ref:nature-nbs-095}} that uses regression to combine and compare findings while adjusting for study characteristics. It aims to reconcile conflicting studies or confirm consistent ones. Fixed-effect versions assume the studies do not really differ. Mixed-effect versions allow for variation between them, and are often the most flexible choice. It has been applied to the {{ref:nature-val-019}}, energy and water policy, and price elasticities for water and energy. It is increasingly used to weigh evidence across many cost-benefit studies of a policy.

openers.valuation-methods: Nobody sells a forest or a beach, so putting a number on one takes ingenuity. Economists have two broad routes. One reads value from the choices people actually make, such as the time and money they spend reaching a national park, or the price of a house broken down into its features. The other asks people directly in surveys, an approach important enough that a US panel chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow was convened to judge whether it could be trusted. Between them sit cheaper shortcuts, such as borrowing results from earlier studies or pricing what it would cost to replace something.
openers.valuation-econometrics: Survey answers and observed choices are messy data, and turning them into values takes statistics. This chapter gathers the tools. Some treat choices as partly random; others sort people into hidden groups, or combine findings from many studies. The chapter also meets the traps: values that do not grow with the size of a problem, and distorted answers about goods nobody actually has to pay for. A 1989 disaster in Prince William Sound, Alaska, shows how much can ride on the numbers.

reviews.valuation-methods: Every method in this chapter answers one question: how can a value be found for something nobody sells? Revealed preference methods watch behavior, reading the worth of a park from house prices or travel costs. Stated preference methods such as contingent valuation simply ask, and the NOAA panel set rules for doing it well. Surveys have known weak spots, from the embedding effect to the gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay. Choice modeling refines the asking by making people weigh trade-offs, and all of these feed ecosystem valuation, which puts services such as flood control into numbers policy-makers can compare.
reviews.valuation-econometrics: The chapter's tools start from one idea: people's choices look partly random, so value must be inferred from patterns. Random utility models give that idea shape, and multinomial logit, probit, mixed logit and best–worst scaling turn it into estimates. Latent class models find hidden groups, and meta-regression pools findings across many studies. Yet the data come from people, with scope neglect and hypothetical bias distorting what they say. The Exxon Valdez spill, the first case where contingent valuation surveys priced damages, showed how much can ride on these numbers.
